body_markdown:
Scion has chosen a thoroughly Japanese vehicle to usher in the brand’s revival in North America. The Kei-01 is essentially a rebadged model of Japan’s most popular kei truck, the Daihatsu Hijet (also sold as the Toyota Pixis), and it goes on sale, right-hand-drive and all, next year. Fleets get first dibs. Individuals? “Wait and see,” says Toyota. Price? We’ll have to get back to you on that. Patience may be the better part of valor here, because this is not America’s typical truck, and that is reason to both love it and approach it with clear expectations.


First off: If you’ve never driven a kei truck before (your author hadn’t), it really is fun. It looks like a toy from the outside, but once you swing open the short, light door and get settled behind the full-size steering wheel, it feels less foreign. Nothing inside the car is miniature. The HVAC switches, the plastic-handled shifter, the window switches: They’re all familiar. Materials-wise, everything is hard plastic or rubber, complemented by thin gray carpet and black cloth. Cheap? Yes. Charming in its simplicity? Absolutely. Trucks were born for utilitarian reasons, and in that sense the Kei-01 is purely traditional, down to its rubber mats and above-your-head shelf.


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)

Usually, a manufacturer scrupulously cleans vehicles during a media drive. This kei truck enjoyed no such pampering and looks more honest with the dust and dirt, we think.


In our brief experience driving the Kei-01 on a short dirt-and-gravel loop, it reminded us of a shrunken Subaru. The ride was surprisingly comfortable: The four-wheel-drive truck pounded over the imperfect surface happily, without rattling our teeth. The accelerator pedal is touchy, and stabbing it provokes a surge of torque from the 660-cc three-cylinder that thrums under your butt. No, the engine is not at all powerful, but the vehicle it’s moving is light (likely around 2000 pounds), so it feels peppy at low speeds, even with a CVT. Compared to a UTV, it’s also fairly quiet. The brake pedal is light, and the feedback is minimal, though the little truck hauls down to a stop easily. Most Japanese-market Hijets use front discs and rear drums, though Toyota isn’t yet specifying the setup (or horsepower or torque) for the U.S.-market truck.


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)


The steering feel and turning radius are the trucklet’s most striking aspects: At four turns lock-to-lock, maneuvering small spaces requires a lot of hand-over-hand action. Thankfully, the truck is very responsive. If you’ve never driven one before, you’ll be astounded at how it tucks its tiny little steel wheels under its body and chases its tail like a puppy. Not only can it maneuver in tight spaces, but it can also haul meaningful amounts of stuff into and through tight spaces thanks to a 600-pound payload and the ability to tow “small trailers.” (Again, Toyota’s keeping quiet on specs for now.) The hinged rear and sides of the dropside bed allow access to whatever you’re carrying. The bed doesn’t even rise to waist-height for an adult, so picking stuff out of it or putting stuff into it is easy.


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)


The biggest difference between the U.S.-market Scion Kei-01 and its Daihatsu sibling (aside from the fact that the Scion will be built in Indiana) is the top speed. The only way Toyota can sell a right-hand-drive Japanese-market Daihatsu here without homologating the car is as a Low Speed Vehicle, as[defined by the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.500) , which govern all traits of all the vehicles sold here, down to the location of their turn signals. The LSV rules mandate a top speed of 25 mph. Installing a speed limiter is infinitely cheaper than designing a kei truck to meet the same crash standards as the “compact trucks” we know today. This Scion kei truck is a truly useful pickup, but its range of usefulness isn’t the same as the quarter- or half-tons we drive to work every day on the interstates at 75-plus. This tiny Scion was born for inner-city driving in Japan, and it’s coming to our shores practically unchanged—which is its allure and which also comes with real trade-offs.


So if you are tempted to be indignant that Toyota isn’t selling this straight to the public yet, perhaps consider whether it is the best vehicle for what you want it to do. We are used to vehicles that DO IT ALL, but as any classic car owner can tell you, it’s wise to know what your vehicle is built to do, and what it’s not built to do. Far from being limiting, understanding the limits of your vehicle frees you to enjoy it in the environments in which it excels.


Hagerty editor Stefan Lombard spent a summer driving a 4WD kei truck in such an environment—the cinder backroads of a national park in northern Arizona. “It was the perfect vehicle for puttering around on little patrols, checking up on cultural sites, hauling around signage and cleaning supplies, and generally exploring the woods,” he says. It was a capable little machine, too, he says, so naturally he tested it. “I discovered its limits while climbing a very steep, very rutted hill in 4-lo. Somewhere about three-quarters of the way up, it ran out of steam and I ran out of talent and then had to figure out how to get back down. There was one hairy moment where the thing began to teeter, so I just opened the door and planted my foot on the ground, which kept me upright. Never tried that again.”


[Grace Jarvis](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/grace-jarvis/)


Toyota’s fleet-only sales strategy for this Scion trucklet doesn’t mean you can’t own a kei truck in the U.S. You just can’t buy a *new* one. You can import a “classic” one (without a speed limiter, too) as long as it’s at least 25 years old. You may already live in a state that lets you title, register, and drive them on public roads, too: Last year,[Colorado](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/colorado-becomes-latest-state-to-legalize-kei-vehicles/) joined about 19 other states in legalizing kei trucks. Regulations differ greatly between states, so be sure to do your research before you start seriously shopping.


In our opinion, these are ideal vehicles for farms and ranches. We just wouldn’t take a Kei-01 into town. The drive would probably take forever, and besides, that’s what your full-size pickup is for!
